title: Mountains walking
hook: Dogen's teaching that the blue mountains are always walking

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dogen's instructions for sitting, and your line, let go. Did you drop the grade on something for one breath? Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

A mountain is the stock picture of something that doesn't move. People say steady as a mountain. Yesterday, Dogen told the sitter to settle into steady, unmoving sitting. So it's startling to open another of his essays, the Mountains and Waters Sutra, and find him passing on an old Chan teacher's saying, in paraphrase: the blue mountains are always walking. Not once, long ago. Always. And then he turns it on the reader. Today: mountains walking.
screen: `STEADY AS A MOUNTAIN.` → `THE BLUE MOUNTAINS ARE ALWAYS WALKING.` → `THEN HE TURNS IT ON YOU.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes from. Dogen quotes the line from an earlier Chan teacher, Furong Daokai, and builds an essay around it. The essay is part of his larger collection, the Shobogenzo. Second, what he says about it. In paraphrase: the mountains' walking is just like people's walking. Don't doubt it because it doesn't look like human walking. Then the turn: if you doubt the mountains walking, you don't yet understand your own walking. The puzzle isn't really about rocks. It's about how you see anything at all. Third, a way in. Readers hear this more than one way. Some hear it about time: the mountain you're looking at is never quite the same mountain twice. Wind, water, seasons and light are moving through it, and it's moving through them. Some hear it about seeing: the idea that a mountain sits still, while you're the one going places, is a habit of the mind, not the whole truth. Dogen doesn't settle it for us with a single explanation. He keeps the line strange on purpose. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. It's easy to treat certain things as fixed: a parent, a hometown, a job, one's own personality. That's just how it is. The mountains walking teaching gently loosens that. What looks fixed may be quietly moving. And the self that thinks it's the only thing on the road may be standing still more than it knows.
screen: `AN OLD CHAN LINE, A DOGEN ESSAY.` · `DOUBT THE MOUNTAINS, DOUBT YOUR WALK.` · `TIME, OR A HABIT OF SEEING?` · `WHAT LOOKS FIXED IS STILL MOVING.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAINS WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. If there's a hill, a tree, a building or even a wall you can see, rest your eyes on it. If not, picture a mountain you've seen. Let it be still. Then, slowly, notice what is moving in it or through it: light changing, air, shadows, the life on it, the way your own looking shifts. Don't decide what it means. Just wonder, the way Dogen invites: is it walking? The bell holds the time.
Mountains walking. Dogen's teaching, from an older Chan saying: the blue mountains are always walking, and if you doubt their walking, you don't yet know your own. Today's word.
Your line: the mountains walk. Today, look at one thing you think of as fixed, a street, a person, a habit, and ask what in it is quietly moving. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 1241 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN UP A TREE.`

howItsDone: Zen students read Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra (Sansuikyo) from the Shobogenzo, often in study groups, and teachers return to its line about the walking mountains to unsettle fixed ways of seeing.

what a scholar hears: Dogen quotes Furong Daokai, then adds his own turn: doubt the mountains' walking and you don't yet know your own.

notes: All Sansuikyo material paraphrased: the blue mountains constantly walking (quoted by Dogen from Furong Daokai); mountains' walking like people's walking; not doubting it because it differs from human walking; doubting the mountains' walking means not yet knowing one's own. Confirm against a standard translation.
The two readings (time; habits of seeing) are offered as 'some hear', without ranking; confirm they are fair.
